name: UGC NET Paper 1
fullName: UGC National Eligibility Test – Paper 1 (General Paper on Teaching & Research Aptitude)
conductingBody: National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission
frequency: Twice a year (June and December cycles)
approxCandidates: ≈7–11 lakh registrations per cycle (2024–26). Paper 1 is common to all 80+ subjects.
eligibility: Master's degree (or final year) with 55% (50% for OBC-NCL/SC/ST/PwD/third gender), or a 4-year UG degree with 75%. JRF upper age limit is 30 years (with relaxations). No upper age limit for Assistant Professor or PhD admission.

notification.summary: NTA released the UGC-NET December 2026 information bulletin on 8 Oct 2026. Online applications are open until 28 Oct 2026, and the CBT is scheduled for 14–19 Dec 2026. In the previous June 2026 cycle, results for 84 subjects were declared by late August 2026, with more than 4,000 candidates qualifying for JRF. Fresh exams were held on 9–10 Sep 2026 for English, Commerce and Sociology after errors were found in those papers. Dates come from the bulletin and news reports via web search; the ugcnet.nta.nic.in portal itself could not be reached from the research sandbox.

pattern.notes: In the real exam, Paper 1 (50 Q, 100 marks) and Paper 2 (100 Q, 200 marks) are taken together in one 3-hour sitting with no break. Each question carries 2 marks and there is no negative marking. The 60 minutes shown here is a suggested allocation for Paper 1. Officially the 50 questions are spread over 10 units, typically about 5 each. Comprehension is usually one passage with 5 questions, and Data Interpretation is a table or chart with 5 questions. The question bank holds 60 original questions (6 per unit) for building mocks. Qualification falls into three categories: JRF + Assistant Professor + PhD, Assistant Professor + PhD, and PhD only.

trendAnalysis.summary: This analysis covers June 2024 (re-conducted as a CBT in Aug–Sep 2024), Dec 2024 (held Jan 2025), June 2025, Dec 2025 and June 2026. Paper 1 is consistently rated easy to moderate. Comprehension, DI, ICT and Higher Education are the most scoring units, while Logical Reasoning (Indian logic: pramanas and hetvabhasas, plus syllogisms) and Research Aptitude are the most time-consuming. Recent shifts include more NEP 2020, SWAYAM and Academic Bank of Credits questions in Higher Education, more matching and assertion–reason items, and chronology-based questions. Environment questions increasingly focus on SDGs, COP and India's net-zero commitments. The DI set is usually one table of 5–6 rows needing percentage or ratio calculations.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"For most of human history, knowledge travelled by word of mouth. Epics, genealogies and medicinal recipes were preserved not in libraries but in memory, recited by trained specialists who treated accuracy as a sacred duty. Scholars once dismissed such oral traditions as unreliable, assuming that every retelling must distort the original. Field studies in the twentieth century challenged this view. Researchers found that some communities transmitted long texts across centuries with remarkable fidelity, using rhythm, repetition and strict teacher–student lineages as safeguards. At the same time, oral cultures were never frozen: storytellers adapted episodes to their audiences, adding local heroes or contemporary jokes while keeping the core intact. Writing, when it arrived, did not simply replace memory; it changed what people thought worth remembering. Once a text could be consulted on a shelf, the effort of memorisation seemed wasteful, and the specialist reciter slowly lost his social standing. Today, as digital search makes even written reference instant, some educators worry that a similar shift is under way – not the loss of knowledge itself, but the loss of the habit of holding knowledge within oneself."

Earlier scholars dismissed oral traditions as unreliable because they assumed that:
options: Writing had existed before oral traditions
Oral texts were too short to be useful
Every retelling must distort the original
questions.explanation: The passage says scholars dismissed oral traditions 'assuming that every retelling must distort the original'.

relevance.note: Factual retrieval from passage; passage shorter than NET's ~400 words

"Cities have always been engines of opportunity, but they are also becoming the front line of climate risk. More than half of the world's people now live in urban areas, and the share is still rising. Dense concentrations of concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, producing what scientists call the urban heat island effect. On summer nights, the centre of a large city can remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. The consequences are not evenly shared. Wealthier neighbourhoods often enjoy tree-lined streets, parks and air-conditioned homes, while informal settlements are packed with tin-roofed houses that trap heat and offer little shade. For outdoor workers – street vendors, construction labourers, delivery riders – a heatwave is not an inconvenience but a threat to health and income. Planners have begun to respond. Some cities are painting roofs white to reflect sunlight, restoring lakes and wetlands, and protecting urban forests. questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Science is usually presented to students as a sequence of triumphs: a question is asked, an experiment is performed and an answer is found. Textbooks rarely mention the false starts, the instruments that did not work, or the years in which a promising idea led nowhere. This tidy picture is convenient, but it is also misleading. For every published discovery there are many experiments that failed, and much of what scientists know about how not to proceed is never written down.

The reasons are partly practical and partly cultural. Journals prefer results that are new and positive; a study showing that a drug had no effect, or that an earlier finding could not be reproduced, is harder to publish and brings less recognition. Funding agencies reward productivity measured in papers, and young researchers on short contracts cannot afford to spend a year on work that may never appear in print. As a result, negative results stay in laboratory notebooks, and other groups unknowingly repeat the same unsuccessful experiments, wasting time and money.

The cost is not only financial. When only successful studies are visible, the published record gives an exaggerated impression of how strong an effect is. A medicine that appears effective in five published trials may have failed in five others that were never reported. Doctors, policymakers and the public then make decisions on the basis of a biased sample of evidence.

Some remedies are already being tried. A number of journals now accept 'registered reports', in which the research question and method are reviewed and accepted before the data are collected, so that publication does not depend on the outcome. Online repositories allow researchers to share data and null findings quickly. Some universities have begun to give credit for replication studies when evaluating staff.

Yet changing incentives is only half the task. Students must also learn that failure is an ordinary part of inquiry, not a sign of incompetence. A laboratory course in which every experiment is guaranteed to work teaches technique, but it does not teach science. Allowing students to design experiments that might fail, and asking them to explain what went wrong, may do more to prepare them for research than any number of perfect demonstrations."

According to the passage, negative results often remain unpublished because:
A. journals prefer results that are new and positive
B. funding agencies reward productivity measured in papers
C. negative results are usually based on faulty experiments
D. young researchers on short contracts cannot spend long on work that may not be published
E. laboratory notebooks are confidential documents

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, C and D only
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives journal preference, funding incentives and the insecurity of short contracts. The passage never says negative results are faulty or that notebooks are confidential.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.question: Pointing to a photograph of a boy, Meena says, "His mother is the only daughter of my father." How is Meena related to the boy?
questions.explanation: The only daughter of Meena's father is Meena herself (she is a daughter). So the boy's mother is Meena.

questions.question: A's salary is 25% more than B's salary. By what percentage is B's salary less than A's?
questions.explanation: If B = 100, A = 125. B is less by 25/125 × 100 = 20%. Taking 25% again ignores the change of base.

questions.question: A 60-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 1 : 2?
questions.explanation: Milk = 40 L, water = 20 L. For 1 : 2, water must be 80 L, so add 80 − 20 = 60 L. 80 L is the final quantity, not the amount added.

questions.question: The difference between compound interest and simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹50. The sum is:
questions.explanation: For 2 years, CI − SI = P(R/100)² = P × 0.01 = 50, so P = ₹5,000.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct?
A. A valid deductive argument can have false premises.
B. An argument whose premises and conclusion are all true is always valid.
C. A sound argument is a valid argument with all true premises.
D. Inductive arguments are evaluated as strong or weak rather than valid or invalid.
E. A valid argument can have true premises and a false conclusion.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, C, D and E only
questions.explanation: Validity concerns form, so false premises are possible (A). True premises and conclusion do not guarantee validity (B false). Soundness = valid + true premises (C). Inductive arguments are strong/weak (D). A valid argument cannot have true premises with a false conclusion (E false).

questions.question: "Professor Rao's theory of inflation must be wrong, because he was once fined for a traffic violation." This argument commits the fallacy of:
questions.explanation: The argument attacks the person instead of the theory – ad hominem. A straw man would misrepresent the theory itself.

questions.question:

All researchers are readers.
Some readers are writers.

Conclusions:
I. Some researchers are writers.
II. Some writers are readers.

Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: II is the converse of 'Some readers are writers' and follows. I does not follow: the writers among readers need not include any researchers (undistributed middle).

questions.question: Seismograph : Earthquake :: Anemometer : ?

B. No politicians are honest.
C. Some politicians are honest.

questions.explanation: The O proposition is false, so its contradictory A ('All politicians are honest') is true. By subalternation the I proposition ('Some politicians are honest') is then true, and the E proposition is false.

C. Not seeing a pot on the floor, one knows that the pot is absent.
D. Knowing that Devadatta is alive and not at home, one concludes that he is somewhere outside.

II. Arthapatti

questions.question: In the Nyaya inference 'Sound is non-eternal, because it is produced, like a pot', the hetu (reason) is:
questions.explanation: Sound is the paksha (subject), non-eternality the sadhya (what is to be proved), 'being produced' the hetu (reason) and the pot the drishtanta (example).

questions.question: 'Sound is eternal, because it is knowable.' According to Nyaya, the reason in this inference is an example of which hetvabhasa?
questions.explanation: Knowability is present both in eternal things and in non-eternal things, so the reason is 'erratic' and does not prove the conclusion – savyabhichara. Viruddha would prove the opposite of the sadhya.

questions.question: 'Fire is cold, because it is a substance.' The fallacy in the reason, according to Nyaya, is:
questions.explanation: The conclusion is contradicted by a stronger pramana – perception shows fire to be hot. A reason whose sadhya is already negated by another pramana is badhita.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the NTA UGC-NET Paper 1 cycles of June 2024 (re-exam Aug–Sep 2024), December 2024 (held January 2025), June 2025, December 2025 and June 2026: NTA question papers with provisional keys where available, plus shift-wise memory-based analyses (PW, Careers360, Aspirant Mitraa) found by WebSearch. Official papers could not be fetched in full, so unit-level frequencies are estimates combined with the writer's own knowledge of recent NET papers. NET routinely uses Match-the-List, sequence and "choose A, B and C only" formats; archetypes describe these patterns in our own words, no real question is reproduced. Frequencies are per 50-question paper.
